title: Agabus and the belt (Acts 21)
hookLine: a prophet ties himself with Paul's belt; Paul goes to Jerusalem anyway
carry: the will of the lord be done
tomorrow: a mob, soldiers, a stairway, and he asks to tell a story…

cards: Pull a belt tight and you feel it at once: the buckle, the pressure, how little room is left. In Caesarea, at the house of Philip the evangelist, a prophet named Agabus walks up to Paul and takes his belt.
The King James calls it a girdle. He ties up his own hands and feet with it, right there in the room. Why?
So everyone can see, and feel, what's coming.

teach.h: SO SHALL THEY BIND THE MAN.
teach.b: Bound in Paul's belt, Agabus speaks: "Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles." This isn't the first warning.

teach.h: KNEES ON THE SHORE AT TYRE.
teach.b: In Tyre, disciples told Paul "through the Spirit" not to go up, and when he left anyway, whole families walked him out of town, and "we kneeled down on the shore, and prayed."
Knees in the sand, then leather around a prophet's wrists. Now the room breaks: "both we, and they of that place, besought him not to go up to Jerusalem."

teach.h: READY NOT TO BE BOUND ONLY.
teach.b: And Paul answers through their tears: "What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus."
Here's the one to tell a friend: Paul never calls the prophet wrong. The warning is true, and he goes anyway. In Acts, a warning shows the cost; it doesn't make the choice.
Then his friends do something hard.
"And when he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, The will of the Lord be done."

teach.h: THE WILL OF THE LORD BE DONE.
teach.b: Not a win, not a loss. People who love him, letting go. Paul goes up, and soon a crowd in the temple seizes him, and Roman soldiers take him into custody.

how: Christians pray "thy will be done" in the Lord's Prayer, and some say "the will of the Lord be done" when they let go of a decision that isn't theirs to make.

games.q: what does “agabus and the belt” mean?
o: a gift Paul gave to the church in Caesarea
a prophet acting out Paul's arrest with a belt
a soldier tying Paul up for the long journey

games.q: the warning in Caesarea — tap the pairs.
p: bound his own hands and feet
the King James word for belt
ready not to be bound only

s: the warning meant Paul shouldn't go
it told him what was coming. he went anyway, eyes open.
Paul's friends kept arguing until he left
we ceased, saying, the will of the Lord be done.
Agabus acted out the warning with Paul's own belt
he bound his own hands and feet with it.

games.q: your older brother has a job offer far away. the pay is good, but your parents warn him the city is lonely and expensive. what fits Acts 21?
o: take the warnings seriously, then decide with eyes open.
turn it down; a warning means it's the wrong path.
go, and stop listening to anyone who worries.
games.why: Paul heard every warning and never called them wrong. then he chose, and his friends let go: the will of the Lord be done.

practice: If you're wearing a belt, a watch strap or laced shoes, rest a hand on it and feel how it holds. Bring to mind one place you sense you're meant to go, along with the warnings people have given you.
Hold the strap and the warnings together for a moment, eyes open, without deciding anything yet.

wordCard.voice: Agabus and the belt. A prophet bound with Paul's own belt, a warning Paul heard, and a road he took anyway.

orig.note: Greek: belt or girdle, the one Agabus took from Paul in Acts 21:11.

carryVoice: Your line: the will of the Lord be done. His friends said it the moment they stopped arguing. Until tomorrow.
